title: 道德經 第七十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 79, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 92. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 79 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 任契 (Trusting to the Tally). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to compose, to patch up, to bring into accord (verb; read hè for 'to answer in sound')
a grudge, resentment nursed against another

sentences.l:
Bring a great grudge into accord —
there is bound to be grudge left over.
sentences.i: Patch up a great enmity, and enmity will always be left over.
sentences.n:
A conditional with nothing to mark it. The first three characters are a bare verb phrase with no subject and no 'if': Chinese sets down a situation and then says what follows from it, and English has to supply the joint. You will meet this on every page — the topic first, the comment after, and no word between them.

和 is a verb here, 'to settle, to bring into accord' — the word used of composing a quarrel. Wang Bi's comment is the whole argument of the chapter in one line: if the tally was not kept clear from the start, the grudge grows great, and by the time you come to soothe it the injury cannot be undone — so something is always left over.

sentences.t:
安可以為善？
是以聖人執左契，

morph.gloss: how? — the interrogative use of the character (elsewhere in this book 安 is 'at rest')
to count as, to be taken for (wéi — not the benefactive wèi)
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither 是 'this' nor 以 'by means of' gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
to grasp, to hold fast to
a tally — a contract cut in two, one half to each party, the notches matching when they are brought together

sentences.l:
How can this count as good?
Therefore the sage holds the left-hand tally,
sentences.i: How can that be called good? And so the sage keeps the left half of the tally
sentences.n:
可以 stays two words — 'can | thereby' — and is not yet the single word 'can' it became in later Chinese; you have met it at chapters 44, 59 and 62. 為 is read wéi, 'count as': the house rule reads 為 as wéi everywhere except where it takes a plain noun in the sense 'for the sake of', which is wèi (chapter 81 has one, three units from the end of the book).

The tally is a real object. A contract was cut across a strip of wood or bamboo, each party keeping half; matching the notches proved the claim. The left half was the creditor's, so to hold it is to hold the claim — and the next line says what the sage does with it. Which half went to which party is not perfectly certain in the sources; Wang Bi says only that holding the left tally is what keeps resentment from arising in the first place.

sentences.t:
而不責於人。
有德司契，

morph.gloss: to press a claim, to dun, to demand what is owed
on, upon (the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb)
potency — the power a thing has by being what it is
to take charge of, to have the management of (the word behind the titles of office)

sentences.l:
and yet does not press claims upon others.
Having potency — in charge of the tally;
sentences.i: and never calls in the debt. The man of potency attends to the tally;
sentences.n:
責 is the dunning word — to go to a man and demand what he owes. The sage holds the half that entitles him to do it and does not do it.

有德 and 無德 have no subject and no 'he who': four characters, 'have potency | manage tally', and the person is left for you to supply. Notice also that 司 is a verb here. It is the character in the old titles of office (司馬, 司空 — the one who manages horses, the one who manages works), and it keeps that flavour: not merely to hold, but to be in charge of.

morph.gloss: to exact, to take what is due — Wang Bi glosses it 司人之過, keeping the account of other people's faults; the character is also the name of the Zhou tithe, a tenth part of the harvest

sentences.l: lacking potency — in charge of exaction.
sentences.i: the man without it attends to exacting.
sentences.n:
徹 is the hard word in the chapter. Wang Bi, whose commentary sits beside this text and is our first guide, glosses it 司人之過 — keeping the account of other people's faults, watching for the failure that lets you make a demand. The character is also the name of the Zhou tax, a tithe of one part in ten, and on that reading the man without potency is simply the tax-collector, going out to take. The English above is worded so that both can stand, because either way the contrast is the same: one man holds the claim and waits, the other goes out to collect.

契 and 徹 both belong to the Old Chinese 月 rhyme group, so the two halves of the couplet chimed. In Mandarin (qì / chè) nothing of that is left.

sentences.t:
天道無親，
常與善人。

morph.gloss: kin, blood relations; and so partiality, favour shown to one's own
to side with, to be on the side of (yǔ; the same character is 'to give' in chapter 81)

sentences.l:
Heaven's way has no kin;
abidingly it is with good men.
sentences.i: The way of heaven has no favourites; it is always on the side of the good.
sentences.n:
天道 is left as two words here, as at chapter 47 — 'heaven's way', a plain possessive with no particle between the two nouns, which Classical Chinese allows freely.

無親 is 'has no kin'. The claim is not that heaven is cold but that it has no relations to favour: no family, therefore no favouritism. The line looks like a proverb older than this book: the Zuo Commentary quotes it from the Zhou Documents as 皇天無親，惟德是輔, 'august heaven has no kin; it aids potency and nothing else'.

與 here is 'to be with, to side with'. Hold on to that, because the last chapter of the book uses the same character for 'to give'.
